Dumbo : The Albino Elephant calf

By: Sinethemba Nogude | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Rescued from a snare trap near Kruger in January this year ( she had been trapped for about 4 days) , Khanyisa is a rare albino elephant calf who is stealing the hearts of people

Unique Selling Point:
On 6 January 2020, HERD received a four-month-old female albino elephant that was found trapped in a
snare with severe injuries.
Her wounds indicated that she had been trying desperately to free herself for a few days. She had severe
lacerations around the back of her ears and neck that stretched around her mouth and cheeks. The top
section of her right ear had been sliced off. There was no sign of her herd anywhere.
The elephant was first taken into the care of the team at Care for Wild Rhino Sanctuary in Mpumalanga. She
was stable, but her injuries were extensive. Their veterinary team attended to the calf's wounds as our HERD
elephant care team departed immediately to assist in caring for her that vital first night, ahead of transporting
her to HERD in Limpopo Province.
HERD Founder, Adine Roode and wildlife vet, Ben Muller, joined them the next morning, once all correct
permits were in place, to collect the calf and transfer her to HERD. It was a three-hour journey.
By the evening of 7 January, the injured calf arrived safely at HERD in the Kapama Private Game Reserve, the
elephant settled in quickly, with Lammie, HERD’s resident companion sheep for company.
As an albino, the elephant is more visible in the bush, and thus susceptible to attacks by predators. It also
means that her eyes are more sensitive to light. However, albino elephants have been known to survive in
the wild.
Her first morning at HERD, the young calf took her first walk in the early morning light, and Adine decided to
name her "Sunshine". Dr. Rogers suggested the closest translation in the local Shona language is "Khanyisa",
meaning “Light/Sunshine”.

Summary:
Wildlife vets Dr. Peter Rogers of Provet Wildlife Services has continued to assist in attending to Khanyisa’s
wounds, check-ups, and fluid and vitamin administrations.
2
With any elephant calf, their delicate nature has proven them to be one of the most difficult wild animals to
hand-rear. Our team are facing the additional challenge of Khanyisa’s severe wounds and albinism. So each
day her health continues to improve, is a victory.
Three weeks have passed since she has been in HERD's care, and Khanyisa continues to improve each day, her
wounds are healing, her eyes are bright and she is very alert and inquisitive. She arrived weighing 124KG and
her weight on 28 January was 138KG, a welcomed 14KG weight gain. She is an incredibly brave and resilient
little elephant, and she has captured our hearts and of many around the world too.
The proximity of the neighbouring adult Jabulani Herd have been reassuring to the little one, and once she
has fully healed, we will start with the reintegration process with her new family, under the guidance of an
expert elephant advisory team.

Press Release:


Khanyisa – The Albino Elephant
Trapped in a snare for several days without food or water and seriously injured, Khanyisa – a rare albino elephant calf didn’t stand a chance. At just six months old, her herd eventually abandoned her, leaving her to battle the elements alone. Now with a little help from some friends, she’s on the road to recovery.
Producer: Sinethemba Nogude | Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


Script: Khanyisa

- Opening night visuals ( gentle eerie music)– sounds of elephants rumbling-

V/O They are Africa’s gentle giants, revered in local folklore for their power and graceful nature.The African Elephant once ranged across most of Southern Africa, but in the 19th century the ivory trade decimated the population.

V/O And in recent times poaching and conflict with humans has led to some unfortunate casualties, resulting in an increased number of orphaned elephants.

V/O Elephants are highly social animals and need the herd to survive.

V/O After seeing the profound impact caused by mankind Adine Roode, a keen conservationist took the bold step to build the Hoedspruit Elephant Rescue and Development centre , a dedicated elephant orphanage in limpopo that provides a unique adoptive family structure for once herdless elephants .

Link Derek On the 8th of January , the orphanage took this baby albino elephant into their care , she’d been caught in a snare and badly injured , no sign of her herd.

Upsound : So we start early, she is on two hourly bottles,just before six, she actually comes out, she depends on the weather , if its cold she will stay in a bit longer, we try take her out early morning.then during the harsh sun hours we take her inside.

Link : Albino elephants are much more rare in African elephants than in Asia, they are redish brown or pink in colour and may suffer from vision impairment and skin problem because of sun exposure

V/O Because of her highly sensitive eyes and skin Roode and her team use an umbrella to simulate shade Khanyisa would have gotten from her mother in the wild.

Upsound Adine: She actually closes her eyes during the day time and a lot of times if something is low she will walk into it because she doesn’t see it –she closes her eyes

Upsound Peter Rogers : I heard she was an Albino elephant or a pink elephant, but it really didn’t prepare me for what I saw.

V/O Experienced wild life veterinarian Dr Peter Stewart Rogers was one of the first people to be called in to the orphanage to examine Khanyisa.

Upsound Peter: Nine times out of ten she would have died, she would’nt have been found , its just luck.
V/O Khanyisa was initially taken to Care for Wild Rhino Sactuary in Mpumalanga where she was stabilised , before a rescue team from the orphanage was despatched to relocate her to the elephant orphanage. 21 year old Khensani Ngobeni, a trainee elephant carer never left her side during this trying time.
Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: When we went to fetch Khanyisa.

Upsound Khensani Ngobeni :We didn’t know we didn’t know what kind of baby she was,

Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: we just heard that she was cut by a wire.

Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: So when we got there , we found that she was badly hurt and scary.

Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: So when we got there he came close to us trying to figure out,
Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: what kind people we are by smelling us,

Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: because she had had just arrived where we found her.

Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: Then we sat down with him. It was me, Joshua and Juan.

Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: So we stayed with him trying to check the extent of his injury.

Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: So she would drink the milk and sometimes fall asleep in 2 hours intervals,

V/O After a tough night,the mission was a success.

Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: Then in the morning we woke up with her and she was fine,
Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: she didn’t give us a problem the whole night.

Upsound Khensani Ngobeni: When they checked her they also cleaned her wounds.

Upsound Peter : that snare was right through her mouth, like this tore into her cheeks there and went in right through the ears , she was unable to drink unable to eat and she was apparently on her own for six days , when she arrived she was incredibly dehydrated.I am surprised she survived really.

Upsound Peter: Upsound: Its an uphill battle from day one , she came in with three factors that were against her , firstly this life threatening snare wound , secoundly her colour very susceptible to being sunburnt and thirdly to get her onto the right milk formula because it varys from one individual to the next.
Upsound: Having the right diet helps the body heal better , we are fortunate in the sense that we have got wild elephants here surrounding her in the reserve itself, so what we do is get the fresh dung and squeeze it out, not that fluid and the dung contains the microorganisms that you would find in an elephant gut, the call it TRANSFAUNATION, where you are supplementing the gut with natural bacteria.Its essential.

V/O Since then Khanyisa is back on her feet, her eyes bright, is a bundle of joy and is always in a playful mood. She is now also making friends, Lammie the resident sheep at the orphanage has become a close companion, they even share a room.

V/O for the past twenty two years , the orphanage has taken in elephants from all over southern Africa , and their numbers have grown to a family of 17 elephants- called the Jabulani HERD.

Upsound Derek: You want to introduce her to the heard quite soon
Upsound Adine I want to introduce her as soon as possible, the sooner the better
Upsound Derek : It’s a perfect set up here , I mean the adoptive herd,
Upsound Derek : It is amazing , I mean I wouldn’t be able to do what I do if we didn’t have the herd, I mean they play a huge role, in accepting the babies, but also in the social wellbeing, a lot of people will ask , aren’t you releasing them, at this stage if I had to say its inhumane to release them just like that, because who do you choose, they are a family structure, Once you have a big enough family… reintegrate them in different areas, in a way I am already looking at a five to ten year model on areas , opportunity to reintergrate them.

Link; The Jabulani Herd is made up of orphaned elephants, and so far they have been welcoming of new comers , giving the young ones the family structure that they depend on.

V/O Elephant Manager Owen Dube, has been working with orphaned elephants for 15 years , she will oversee Khanyisa’s transition into her newly adopted family.

Upsound Owen, Its so amazing to see these elephants accept a new baby elephant of which in the whild it doesn’t happen, they are also orphaned elephants and they learn to accept each others as individuals , so for this baby to be introduced its very nice because she still has that memory of the family, she is also smelling that I do have a family around her , so for her to be introduced around here , it will be very nice as soon as possible.so that she know I still have a family.

V/O Currrently Khanyisa is separated from her soon to be family in order for her wounds to be fully healed.Introduction into her adoptive family will be a gradual process, but for now the toddler has other pressing matters.
